Conjura is built on one bet: that AI can be used as far as it will go in mathematical research, provided what comes out is held to a standard that does not care where it came from.

## Why this exists

Two problems. The first is old, and the second the field made for itself.

- **Research collides instead of compounding.** Results are produced in isolation, so partial progress is rediscovered more than once and the same dead ends are walked into by people who never learn of each other's attempts. Conjura's answer is a public, durable record of what has been tried, what is resolved, and what is still stuck.
- **Venue policy aims at authorship rather than verification.** Read at source on 16 August 2026, [Crypto 2026](https://crypto.iacr.org/2026/aipolicy.php), [Asiacrypt 2025](https://asiacrypt.iacr.org/2025/aipolicy.php) and [TCC 2026](https://tcc.iacr.org/2026/aipolicy.php) each say they will "generally follow the ACM Policy on the use of AI tools". ACM and IEEE converge on the same shape: no AI author, humans accountable, substantive generation disclosed. None of that is unreasonable, and Conjura does not argue with it.
- **The operative clause is a limit on degree.** A work must be "not primarily the result of the tool's generative capabilities". That is the line this site crosses on purpose. "Primarily" has no operational definition, no reviewer can recover it from a finished manuscript, and none of the three policies describes a way to detect a breach or a consequence for one.
- **So the disagreement is narrow, and it is about what disclosure *is*.** Not "they forbid AI and we allow it", which would be false and easy to check. At a venue, disclosure is a sentence in an acknowledgements section: unverifiable, and attached to a paper judged whole. Here it is per artifact and machine-checked.
- **The ambition, stated plainly.** Cryptology should have a venue for work that is openly and substantially AI-assisted, judged on whether its results survive checking rather than on the model's share of the drafting. The IACR already publishes [Communications in Cryptology](https://cic.iacr.org/), a real and well-run venue; this is a difference of editorial posture, not a complaint. Conjura is a beginning of one, not the thing itself.

## What we are building

Some of this exists and some does not. The difference is marked rather than blurred.

- **Working in the open.** Conjectures are explored in public rather than in private notebooks, with intermediate states shared as they happen. A recorded dead end saves someone else the time of rediscovering it.
- **Rigour, with the exposition that makes it usable.** Machine-checked proofs and precise statements wherever feasible, kept alongside the informal explanation of why a result is true and why it was hard. Formal artifacts alone do not make a result understood.
- **Disclosure per artifact, and one gap in it.** The [prompts](/prompts/index.qmd) are published in full and every statement, proof and formalization records whether a human or a model produced it. The session logs are not: each statement folder has a `sessions/` directory for the raw transcript, and as of 16 August 2026 every one of them is empty. That gap stays written here until it closes.
- **Who gets to do the work.** Access to capable models is now a real input to research output and is not evenly held. If results track available compute, the field's output tracks budgets rather than ideas, and it does so invisibly, because nobody publishes the attempts they could not afford to run. Conjura redistributes no compute today; publishing its tooling is the only levelling act currently in effect.
- **Four things that are not built.** Bounties attached to open problems, claimable once a resolution is verified. Idle API capacity pointed at the backlog instead of expiring unused. Distributed multi-model compute for problems no single account should carry. And the journal above. Directions, not features.

## How anything here is judged

One commitment, applied to particular decisions: use these tools as far as they go, and hold what comes out to a standard that does not care where it came from. Neither half survives alone.

- **A badge can understate, never overstate.** What has been machine-verified or independently reviewed is tracked separately from what merely reads well. AI has made it cheap to produce writing that reads as rigorous without anyone having checked it, and writing more carefully does not fix that: a fabricated citation can be written as carefully as a real one.
- **A negative result keeps its page.** A withdrawn statement becomes a tombstone; a disproof of an easy special case is filed as solved rather than dropped as an embarrassment. A record showing only successes is a highlight reel, not a record of progress.
- **Attribution changes the record, never the standard.** Whether a human or a model produced something, the record says so and the thing is checked the same way. This is the precise point of difference with the venue policies: they ask how much of the work the model did, which has no measurable answer; Conjura asks what has been checked, which has both an answer and a gate.
- **Verification is work worth crediting.** Reviewing a proof has never carried the reward that producing one does. The site designs against that: adversarial stress-testing before a human sees a submission, a reviewer's name permanently attached to what they checked, and more than one model, since one model's blind spots applied to both the writing and its own review are still one perspective wearing two hats.
- **Publishing in the open has one exception.** A result that breaks something deployed is disclosed privately first. Nearly nothing here is in that category, but an agent working a conjecture cannot tell in advance whether it is producing a separation or a practical break. The exception suspends *when* something is published, never *whether*, and its scope is written down in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/crypto-conjura/crypto-conjura.github.io/blob/main/SECURITY.md).
- **What is not built is said plainly.** An idea worth exploring and a shipped feature are different things, and a roadmap reading as more finished than it is would undo the rest of this page.
- **[This site has not been reviewed either.]{#this-site-has-not-been-reviewed-either}** Everything above grades the research artifacts; this grades the container. The prose on every page, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the schema, the scripts, the templates, the encyclopedia stubs and this page were generated by an AI. A human directed, prompted and refined all of it, so it is not unsupervised output and responsibility is not deferred by saying so. But it has not had thorough independent review by anybody, and it should have, from more than one reviewer. That notice narrows only as review actually happens, naming which part, by whom and when; it does not soften with time, with more edits, or without something having been checked.
